I. KEY FINDINGS
1. Nonresident Alien Shareholder — HIGH RISK
The Historical Shareholder Schedule reflects that on June 1, 2022, shareholder Gregory A. Beaumont transferred 100,000 shares to Carrie Canuck, a Canadian resident. A nonresident alien is an ineligible S‑Corporation shareholder. This event caused an automatic termination of S‑Corporation status as of the transfer date.
2. Pro Rata Distribution Compliance — HIGH RISK
Historic distributions do not conform to required ownership percentages, producing recurring disproportionate distributions. The IRS may treat repeated deviations as evidence of a prohibited second class of stock.
3. Debt‑Equity Characterization and Shareholder Loans — HIGH RISK (Documentation Missing)
No shareholder loan agreements, repayment schedules, general ledger entries, or basis tracking schedules were provided. Given the instruction to treat missing documents as high risk, this category is classified accordingly. The absence of documentation significantly increases the likelihood of IRS recharacterization of advances as equity, which may create a second class of stock.

4. K‑1 Accuracy and Records — MODERATE RISK
Several K‑1s lack ownership percentages, and 2024 K‑1s list individuals who do not appear in the stock ledger. These inconsistencies suggest governance gaps that increase audit exposure.
5. Governance and Corporate Formalities — MODERATE RISK
Multiple versions of the historical shareholder schedule (Rev A/B/C) reflect inconsistent treatment of 2022–2023 transfers. Inconsistent ledgers weaken Summit’s ability to substantiate S‑status compliance.
6. Tax Return Consistency (1120‑S) — LOW RISK
Forms 1120‑S appear internally consistent with the operating history. No accumulated earnings and profits or built‑in gains issues were identified.
